title: Network policies
summary: By default every pod can talk to every pod. Change that.

steps.title: Default allow, then isolate
body: Out of the box the pod network is flat: any pod can reach any pod in any namespace. A **NetworkPolicy** selects pods and, once a pod is selected by any policy for a direction (ingress or egress), **only traffic some policy allows** gets through in that direction.
podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: postgres } }   # protects these pods
Result: postgres pods accept TCP 5432 from `shop-api` pods in `shop`, and nothing else. Pods no policy selects are unaffected.
> **Tip:** Policies are enforced by the network plugin (Calico, Cilium, Azure NPM...). On a cluster whose CNI does not support them, they are accepted and **silently ignored**.
A common baseline is a **default deny** per namespace (`podSelector: {}` with no ingress rules) and then explicit allows.

steps.prompt: Only policy in namespace `shop`: the one on the card. Which connections succeed? (Postgres listens on 5432.)
items: postgres pod to a `shop-api` pod on 8080 (no policy selects shop-api)
steps.explain: A bare `podSelector` in `from` only means pods in the policy's own namespace. Use `namespaceSelector` to allow other namespaces. Policies select the *destination* for ingress; the shop-api pods themselves are not restricted.

steps.prompt: You add a default-deny ingress policy to namespace `shop`. Suddenly the Gateway's proxy pods (in namespace `gateway`) return 504s for every site. Why?
options: The proxy's traffic into `shop` pods is now denied; you must allow it with a `namespaceSelector` for the `gateway` namespace
Default deny also blocks DNS for the controller
steps.explain: Default deny means *everything* into those pods, including from the Gateway's proxy and from Prometheus scraping metrics.

steps.prompt: Allow traffic into the selected pods from any pod in namespaces labelled `team=frontend`.
Egress default-deny breaks every outbound HTTP call **by name**, even to allowed IPs. What did you forget to allow?
options: UDP and TCP port 53 to the cluster DNS (kube-dns / CoreDNS) pods
steps.explain: Name resolution happens first. Every egress-deny setup needs an explicit DNS allow.

steps.prompt: Ingress isolation in one line. A pod is selected by no policy. What does this print?
steps.explain: Unselected pods stay wide open. Isolation only starts when a policy selects the pod.

steps.prompt: You apply a NetworkPolicy on a kind cluster using its default CNI, and traffic is not blocked at all. Why?
options: The network plugin does not enforce NetworkPolicy, so the object is stored but ignored
Policies take an hour to apply
kind clusters have no pod network
Policies only work on LoadBalancer Services
steps.explain: Install a CNI that enforces policies (Calico, Cilium) when you need to test them locally. Always test that a deny actually denies.

steps.title: Lock a namespace down with NetworkPolicies
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). It enforces NetworkPolicies. In the namespace `shop`, the pods `web` and `debug` can both call the
Service `api`: try `kubectl -n shop exec web -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://api/`.
1. Add a **default-deny** policy for incoming traffic to every pod in `shop`.
2. Then allow exactly one path: pods labelled `app=web` may reach pods labelled `app=api` on TCP port 80.

checks.name: a default-deny ingress policy covers every pod
checks.cmd: kubectl -n shop get networkpolicy -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} and (.spec.policyTypes | index("Ingress")) and ((.spec.ingress // []) | length) == 0) | .metadata.name' | grep -c .
checks.fail: There is no policy with an empty `podSelector`, `policyTypes: [Ingress]` and no `ingress` rules.

checks.name: web reaches api
checks.cmd: kubectl -n shop exec web -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://api/ >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo yes
checks.fail: `web` cannot reach `api`: allow `app=web` to `app=api` on port 80.

checks.name: debug does not
checks.cmd: (kubectl -n shop exec debug -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://api/ >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo reached) || echo blocked

hints: A policy with `podSelector: {}` selects every pod; `policyTypes: [Ingress]` with no `ingress` list allows nothing in.
Policies add up: a second policy with `podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}` and `ingress: [{from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}}], ports: [{port: 80}]}]`.
Write both into one file separated by `---` and `kubectl apply -f` it.
solution: kubectl -n shop exec web -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://api/
kubectl -n shop exec debug -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://api/
steps.explain: Without any policy every pod can reach every other one, across namespaces too. Default-deny plus explicit allows is the production pattern: each allow is an additive rule, and a pod is isolated as soon as one policy selects it. Policies are enforced by the network plugin (here k3s's built-in controller; Cilium or Calico elsewhere): a cluster without one accepts the objects and silently ignores them.
